reason: The sources provide 16 claims with at least two-site verification, supporting a mind-bending story about a runaway star with a light-year-wide bow shock and a dramatic dimming event.
story: Betelgeuse is a celestial fugitive. This massive red supergiant was violently ejected from its birthplace near Orion’s Belt millions of years ago and is now a ‘runaway star’ hurtling through space at 30 kilometers per second. Its journey is so fast it creates a gargantuan bow shock—a shockwave of compressed gas and dust multiple light-years wide. If Betelgeuse replaced our Sun, it would swallow every planet out to Mars. While it recently made headlines for the ‘Great Dimming’ of 2019, where it coughed up a massive dust cloud that obscured its light, its true final act is yet to come. Within the next 100,000 years, this 10-million-year-old giant will explode in a supernova. This death blast will be so powerful it will shine as bright as a half-moon and remain visible in broad daylight for months, providing Earth a safe but spectacular front-row seat to a cosmic cataclysm.
angle: Betelgeuse is a cosmic runaway star ejected from Orion’s Belt, moving so fast it creates a massive bow shock wave multiple light-years wide as it plows through the galaxy.

claims.claim: Betelgeuse is a red supergiant star located in the constellation of Orion.
It is normally one of the ten brightest stars in the night sky.
If placed at the center of the solar system, it would engulf the orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth, and Mars.
Betelgeuse is a runaway star that was ejected from its birthplace near the stars in Orion's Belt.
The star is moving through space at a speed of 30 km/s.
Its movement creates a bow shock where its stellar wind crashes into the interstellar medium.
The bow shock is multiple light-years wide.
Betelgeuse is roughly 10 million years old.
It is expected to end its life in a supernova explosion within approximately 100,000 years.
When it goes supernova, it will shine as bright as the half-moon.
The supernova explosion will be visible from Earth in broad daylight.
Starting in late 2019, the star underwent a record-breaking dimming event.
During the Great Dimming, it dropped from being a top-10 brightest star to 21st brightest.
The dimming was caused by a massive dust cloud formed from material ejected by the star.
The name Betelgeuse resulted from a 13th-century mistranslation of its original Arabic name.
It is the brightest star in the night sky when viewed at near-infrared wavelengths.

disputed: Width of the bow shock: S1 and S2 cite 4 light-years, while S3 and S6 cite 3 light-years; the script should use 'roughly three to four light-years wide.'
Arabic meaning: S1 interprets the original name as 'Hand of al-Jawzā', while S2 interprets it as 'Armpit of al-Jawzā'; the script should attribute this to translation nuances.
Distance: Estimates range from 400 to 700+ light-years due to measurement difficulty; the script should note it is approximately 500-600 light-years away.
Supernova timing: S1, S2, and S5 suggest within 100,000 years, but S7 mentions estimates as far out as a million years; the script should emphasize the 100,000-year estimate but mention uncertainty.
